page: Microsoft Azure F4-1ams_v7 is an x86_64 virtual machine instance powered by an AMD processor and virtualized on Microsoft Hyper-V. It provides 1 dedicated vCPU alongside 32.0 GB of system memory, establishing a dense 32.0 GB memory-to-core ratio. The configuration does not include local disk storage or hardware GPU acceleration, relying on remote disk solutions such as Azure Premium Storage for persistent data operations.

Architecturally, this instance operates as a constrained-core configuration within the Fams_v7 family. By allocating a full 32.0 GB memory block to a single virtual processor, it decouples extensive memory capacity from multi-core processor requirements. This architecture presents a clear trade-off: parallel and multi-threaded throughput is restricted to a single processing execution thread, making the instance unsuitable for core-heavy parallel calculations.

From an infrastructure and cost perspective, the F4-1ams_v7 offers resource efficiency for workloads constrained purely by memory capacity rather than compute throughput. It prevents the overprovisioning of compute resources and mitigates per-core software licensing expenses. Best-fit workloads include small-footprint in-memory caches, memory-resident database nodes with low concurrent query volume, single-threaded analytical tasks, and staging environments.
description: Microsoft Azure F4-1ams_v7 is an x86_64 virtual machine based on AMD processor architecture under Microsoft Hyper-V virtualization. Designed as a memory-intensive, constrained-core option within its series, the instance supplies 1 dedicated vCPU paired with 32.0 GB of RAM, yielding an exceptionally high 32.0 GB per vCPU ratio. It operates without integrated local storage or GPU accelerators, relying on Premium Storage capabilities for persistent disk operations. This structural design isolates memory scale from core expansion, making the server well suited for workloads that demand high memory capacity but modest processing concurrency, such as memory-resident databases, caching layers, low-concurrency data pipelines, and memory-intensive development environments. Qualitatively, it delivers resource efficiency by minimizing core allocation and related software licensing overhead while maintaining substantial memory headroom.
